content: For the purpose of formalising the theory of real-rooted polynomials, I need a definition of interleaving lists: For a linear order P, l : List P interleaves l' : List P if l'.length is either l.length or l.length + 1 and its first element is less than l''s first element and greater than l''s second element, its second element is less than l''s second element and greater than l''s third element etc...

To prove properties of the interleaving relation, it is useful to have the operation of interleaving two lists. As explained above, one should expect to sensibly interleave l into l' only if l'.length is either l.length or l.length + 1.
I have PRed both the relation and the operation in #39870 and also batteries#1853.
Now the question is: are there more people out there caring about interleaving lists? or do you interlace/intersperse/alternate them instead?

In the parsing universe, these operations are called sepBy, endBy, sepEndBy, etc. However, these are about deconstructing interleaved lists, so there's no reason for constructing interleaved lists to follow the same taxonomy.
We have docs#List.intersperse and docs#List.intercalate. Somewhat unclear to me how "interlace" would differ from "interleave"...
Indeed, I predict that I will never learn the difference between "intersperse", "intercalate", "interlace", "interleave", are there more? They are nearly synonyms to me, a non-native speaker.
If it helps this is also true for me, a native speaker.

I think there's two/three approaches to this (and some generalisations over other monads).

You can take what I might call the "eager" approach. I've got two lists l, l'. I take an element from the first and put it behind the first element of the second, and recurse. If I ever can't do this - because one is empty - I just stop. So eagerInterLeave [0, 1, 7] [1, 2, 3, 5, 6] = [1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 7]. You could also define this the other way round.

You can take the "lazy" approach. You do the same thing, but if one list is ever empty, you just return the other list. lazyInterLeave [0, 1, 7] [1, 2, 3, 5, 6] = [1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 7, 5, 6].

Finally you could go "if I don't have a first element in one, but do have in the other, I will indeed place the element I do have in the right place, but then I stop". Call this, IDK, mid.
midInterLeave [0, 1, 7] [1, 2, 3, 5, 6] = [1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 7, 5].
(Or I suppose you could say that interleaving [] into [a] gives [a], but interleving [a] into [] gives [].)

My point is that clearly when the two lists are the same size it's obvious what to do. When they're one apart then you can sensibly interleve the smaller into the larger, that's obvious. I think it still makes conceptual sense to do it outside there - even if it's junk for @Yaël Dillies - but I think there's distinct choices.
Sounds like zip then flatten.
Yeah, I think that is not an unreasonable definition (though one might want to define it not using that). But I think this is not the one @Yaël Dillies wants - because [] [a] then goes to [].

Incidentally I think List.intercalate has a completely unhelpful name - flatIntersperse would be better. Actually intersperse itself would maybe be better if you could select the interval of interspersing, but that seems like a strech goal. Clearly interleave and intersperse are related by something like "intersperse is when you interleve replicate".

Notably intersperse k l is indeed [] on l = [] and [a] on l = [a] - i.e. you need at least two elements to the input before you start seeing the interspersed list. intersperse k [a, b] = [a, k, b]. So actually that shows you a real subtlety - [a] and [k] should interleve to give [a, k] but that isn't an output that intersperse can give (with input length n the output is length 2*n - 1).
In contrast zip then flatten can only I think give even length outputs by default.

I'm switching to semantics for a bit, so I will pause the nomenclature discussion by temporarily calling the operation zoo...

The main question when calling zoo a b should the head of the result be the first item of a or the first item of b?

  • Yaël's implementation chooses b. That makes sense if we want a.zoo b to mean "interleave elements of a between elements of b.
  • The opposing view is to choose a. That makes sense if we want a.zoo b to mean "interleave elements of b between elements of a.
  • There is always the option to add @[pp_nodot] to force programmers to use zoo a b or zoo b a to their purpose, whether we choose a or b.

These options leave open the question of what the last item is in zoo a b. If we start with a and b runs out before a, should we add another a item? Similarly if we start with b. So the next question is whether zoo [] b or zoo a [] should return an empty list or try to get the first item from the other list?

Dot notation may not help us here - I feel that the dot ought to apply to the thing being acted upon, but this isn't necessarily the thing that is the first argument!
You might also want to handle the singleton cases differently.
It seems the version in the PRs is the binary one; do we want the n-ary one, which is essentially "transpose"?
For transpose you're implicitly assuming a dense matrix, this does not yet exist in Batteries and is questionably relevant here.

Back to mathematics, do you mean l and l' are the list of roots of f and f' (the derivative of f), respectively? Then we always have #l = #l' + 1. I think maybe def IsInterleaving l l' : Prop := ... suffices, unless you want to join l and l' in some way.

This notion of interleaving appears in representation theory of linearly oriented type A quivers and their higher-dimensional variants, see e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.5437, in there called intertwining. Depending on conventions, variants also use \leq instead of <. Such phenomena also arise in topological data analysis when describing homomorphisms and extensions between interval modules.
My definition is relation-agnostic so it will cover both your <= and < definitions!
